# Jeremiah 1 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Verses 1–3: The Superscription

**v. 1: "These are the words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, one of the priests in Anathoth in the territory of Benjamin."**

- **The "words of Jeremiah" are also the word of the LORD.** This introductory formula ("the words of Jeremiah") only occurs elsewhere in Amos 1:1. The editor departs from the more usual formulas ("burden," "vision," "the word of the LORD which came") to give fuller information about the prophetic writer. (Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/1.htm)
- **Jeremiah's name** has been variously interpreted as "the LORD founds," "the LORD exalts," or "the LORD throws down" (an ambiguity that suits his dual commission to destroy and build). (Enduring Word / Harrison, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-1/)
- **Hilkiah was not the high priest** who found the book of the Law under Josiah (2 Kings 22:8). The priests of Anathoth were of the line of Ithamar, while the high priests from Zadok onward were of Eleazar's line. Jeremiah's Hilkiah was "of the priests that were in Anathoth" — a common priest. (Gill, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-1.html; Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/1.htm)
- **Anathoth** was one of the priestly cities (Joshua 21:18), a small village about three miles northeast of Jerusalem, in Benjamin. From its vantage points one could see the walls of Jerusalem. (Constable, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-1.html; Enduring Word / Thompson)
- **"To whom the word of the LORD came"** (v. 2) — this phrase and similar ones occur 157 times in Jeremiah out of 349 times in the entire OT (about 45% of all OT occurrences). (Constable)

**v. 2–3: "…in the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah… through the days of Jehoiakim… until the fifth month of the eleventh year of Zedekiah… when the people of Jerusalem went into exile."**

- **Dates the main period of Jeremiah's ministry:** 627 BC (Josiah's 13th year) to 586 BC (the fall of Jerusalem). This spans roughly 40 years. (Constable; Gill)
- **Josiah was one of Judah's better kings**, zealous for reform. In his eighth year he sought the LORD (2 Chron 34:3). Jeremiah's call in Josiah's 13th year came five years before the book of the Law was found (2 Kings 22:3). (Gill; Enduring Word)
- **Jehoahaz and Jehoiachin are omitted** from the list of kings in v. 3 because their reigns were very short — only three months each. Jehoahaz reigned between Josiah and Jehoiakim; Jehoiachin between Jehoiakim and Zedekiah. (Enduring Word / Harrison; Constable)
- **Josiah had three sons** who became kings: Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah. Jeremiah prophesied under all three. (Gill)
- **"Until the carrying away of Jerusalem captive"** — though Jeremiah also prophesied after the fall (chs. 40–44), this fixes the main period. The exile in the fifth month (Ab, roughly July–August) is still commemorated by Jews as a fast on the 9th of Ab. (Gill; Constable)

---

## Verses 4–10: The Call of Jeremiah

**v. 4: "The word of the LORD came to me, saying:"**

- The change from third person ("to whom," v. 2) to first person ("to me") marks the beginning of Jeremiah's own account of his call. A similar shift occurs in Ezekiel 1:4. (Ellicott)
- Jeremiah had a **personal encounter** with the LORD. Though raised in a godly priestly home, he needed his own direct, personal experience of God's call. (Enduring Word)

**v. 5: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I set you apart and appointed you as a prophet to the nations."**

- **"I knew you"** — this is knowing with special love and affection, not merely omniscience. It is the knowledge of election (cf. Amos 3:2, "You only have I known of all the families of the earth"). (Gill; Ellicott)
- **The predestination of individuals** is a familiar idea in the OT (cf. Isaiah 45:4; 49:1; Psalm 139:16). Ellicott quotes Dean Milman: "No Pelagian ever has or ever will work a religious revolution. He who is destined for such a work must have a full conviction that God is acting directly, immediately, consciously… upon him." (Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/1.htm)
- **"I sanctified thee"** = "I set thee apart for holy uses." The Hebrew *hiqdish* means to separate from all other uses for prophetic ministry. (Ellicott; Constable)
- **Jeremiah existed as a human being during gestation** (cf. Psalm 139:13). His life's purpose predated his biological existence. The thought that his very being was "a conscious part of divine purpose and not an incidental biological occurrence" gave him a special sense of destiny. (Constable / Harrison)
- **"A prophet to the nations"** — not only to Judah. Jeremiah's prophecies include oracles against Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Elam, and Babylon (chs. 46–51). God is "Lord of the nations." (Enduring Word / Feinberg; Constable)
- **John Piper** (Reformed Baptist) emphasizes four acts of God surrounding Jeremiah's birth: God formed him, knew him, consecrated him, and appointed him. Piper says the first reason Jeremiah should not fear is that "his very life is rooted in the unshakable, sovereign purposes of God." (Desiring God, https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/do-not-say-i-am-only-a-youth)
- **Gill** (Reformed Baptist) notes this is not mere omniscience but special electing love — "such a knowledge as had special love and affection joined with it… which is not only before their formation in the womb, but before the foundation of the world, even from all eternity." (Gill)

**v. 6: "Ah, Lord GOD… I surely do not know how to speak, for I am only a child!"**

- **"Ah, Lord GOD"** (Hebrew *'ahah Adonai Yahweh*) is a cry of alarm and pain. The same expression recurs in Jeremiah 4:10; 14:13; 32:17. It is "expressive of mourning and complaint." (Ellicott; Gill)
- **"I am a child"** — the Hebrew word *na'ar* describes anyone from infancy to young manhood (cf. Genesis 34:19; 41:12; 1 Kings 3:7). Jeremiah was probably about 20 years old, with estimates ranging from 16 to 25. He felt too young and inexperienced for such a weighty office. (Constable; Ellicott)
- **"I cannot speak"** — like Moses (Exodus 4:10), Jeremiah pleads lack of eloquence and skill in public speaking. Unlike Moses, however, "Jeremiah really was young… and inexperienced." (Enduring Word / Kidner)
- **There is a parallel with Moses**: both claim inadequacy as speakers, both were rejected by their hearers. Jeremiah's contemporaries could have mistaken him for "the prophet like Moses" of Deuteronomy 18:18. (Constable)

**v. 7: "Do not say, 'I am only a child.' For to everyone I send you, you must go, and all that I command you, you must speak."**

- **God refused Jeremiah's excuse.** Though Jeremiah's protest was factually true (he was young), it was **irrelevant** — because the authority was God's, not Jeremiah's. (Enduring Word; Constable)
- **"Thou shalt go… thou shalt speak"** — thoughts of self are "altogether out of place in one who has received a Divine commission. Jeremiah's duty is simple obedience." (Ellicott)
- **God doesn't accept age as a barrier**: He used young David, John the Baptist (filled with the Spirit from the womb, Luke 1:15), Timothy (1 Tim 4:12), and many others. (Enduring Word)
- **Piper**: The second reason Jeremiah should not fear is that "God's authority, not his own, is behind his going and his speaking." When Jeremiah speaks God's words, judgment will break down and promises will build up — "not because of young Jeremiah… but because the word of God is powerful." (Desiring God)

**v. 8: "Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you," declares the LORD.**

- **Jeremiah had two reasons to fear**: his youth and his hard message. But God's presence was greater than both. (Enduring Word)
- This promise echoes God's assurance to many OT figures (Genesis 15:1; Numbers 21:34; Deuteronomy 31:6–8; Joshua 1:9). "The Lord always supports the servants whom He sends on His missions." (Constable)
- **Gill**: "Be not afraid of their faces" — their stern looks, frowning brows, and angry countenances which would threaten destruction and death. (Gill)
- **Piper**: The third reason for courage is that "God will be with him to deliver him." Piper applies this to all believers: "God's presence and approval is more valuable than all the accolades of men." (Desiring God)

**v. 9: "Then the LORD reached out His hand, touched my mouth, and said to me: 'Behold, I have put My words in your mouth.'"**

- **The touching of the mouth was a visionary experience**, not purely metaphorical — analogous to Isaiah's inaugural vision where a seraph touched his lips with a coal (Isaiah 6:6–7). However, in Isaiah the act symbolized **purification**, while here it symbolizes **the communication of a prophetic message**. Ellicott notes this distinction and suggests "Isaiah had attained a deeper insight into the spiritual regeneration needed by the prophet." (Ellicott)
- **A real experience**: the touching was "a palpable pledge of His support." (Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-1.html)
- **God touched Jeremiah's mouth not to make him feel qualified, but to put His words there** — the power came from God's presence, not Jeremiah's ability. (Enduring Word)
- **This is a powerful way of visualizing** that the LORD Himself would participate in all Jeremiah would undertake. (Constable)
- **Gill**: It "was signified by the preceding symbol" that "what he should speak should not be his own words, but the words of the Lord." He could therefore speak "with great freedom and boldness." (Gill)

**v. 10: "See, I have appointed you today over nations and kingdoms to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant."**

- **"I have set thee"** — literally, "I have made thee an overseer or vicegerent" (cf. Genesis 41:34; Judges 9:28). Jeremiah is appointed to announce God's will over nations. (Ellicott; Constable)
- **The six verbs**: four destructive (*uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow*) and two constructive (*build, plant*). This reflects the predominantly negative emphasis of Jeremiah's ministry. "He did comparatively little of this constructive preaching and a great deal of the destructive kind." (Enduring Word / Thompson; Constable)
- **The pattern of the spiritual life**: "God has first to remove the sin before the sinner can begin to grow in grace." (Constable / Harrison)
- **Jeremiah pronounces judgment that fulfills itself** — the prophetic word is effective (cf. Jeremiah 5:14; Isaiah 55:11). "The word of God is a power that carries out His will… it is a hammer that breaks rocks in pieces" (Jer 23:29). (Ellicott; Constable / Keil)
- **Gill** notes that the destructive verbs may be understood "of the destruction of the Jews by Nebuchadnezzar, of their temple, city, and nation," while "to build, and to plant" may apply to "the building of the temple, and the planting of the Jews in their own land, after their return from captivity." (Gill)

---

## Verses 11–12: The Vision of the Almond Branch

**v. 11: "Jeremiah, what do you see?" — "I see a branch of an almond tree."**

- **Before Jeremiah could speak for God, he had to be a seer.** "The name for a prophet, in the olden time, was a 'seer' — a man who could see… with spiritual insight." (Spurgeon, https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-lesson-of-the-almond-tree)
- **Spurgeon**: "Before you can make an impression upon another person's heart, you must have an impression made upon your own soul. You must be able to say, concerning the truth, 'I see it,' before you can speak it." (Quoted in Enduring Word)
- **Jeremiah saw not merely a generic rod but specifically "a rod of an almond tree"** — he had "powers of discernment and discrimination which are most needful in the Lord's servants." (Spurgeon)
- **The almond was the first tree to bloom in spring** (blossoming in January in Israel). Anathoth remains a centre for almond growing to this day. (Enduring Word / Thompson; Ellicott)
- **Simplicity of the vision**: "We might have thought that, as a preparation for his prophetical work, he would have seen mysterious wheels full of eyes, or flaming seraphs… Instead of this, Jeremiah simply sees a rod of an almond tree." (Spurgeon, quoted in Enduring Word)

**v. 12: "You have observed correctly… for I am watching over My word to accomplish it."**

- **The Hebrew wordplay**: "almond tree" is *shaqed*; "watching" is *shoqed*. Both come from a root meaning "to be wakeful." The almond is the "wakeful tree" — the first to wake from winter's sleep. God is likewise "wakeful" over His word. (Ellicott; Constable; Enduring Word)
- **"I will hasten my word to perform it"** (KJV) — the almond does not delay in blooming; it is "in haste to blossom and bear fruit." So God is "quick to fulfill His word." (Spurgeon)
- **Spurgeon's application**: "The almond tree sets an example to all who would be like God. He hastens His word to perform it; oh, that you and I would be in haste to perform our word!" (Spurgeon)
- **The first lesson of Jeremiah's training**: a prophet must first *see* truth in his own soul before he can speak it to others. (Enduring Word)
- **This vision stresses the ultimate effectiveness** of Jeremiah's ministry: God will watch over His word to bring it to pass. (Constable)

---

## Verses 13–16: The Vision of the Boiling Pot

**v. 13: "I see a boiling pot, and it is tilting toward us from the north."**

- **"A boiling pot"** (Hebrew *sir*): a cauldron used for cooking or washing. It is boiling with fire underneath, and the opening is tilted southward — about to pour its scalding contents onto Judah. (Constable; Enduring Word)
- **The Hebrew clarifies** that a strong wind was blowing, making the fire hot and causing the pot to boil over. (Constable)
- **Gill**: The Targum paraphrases "I see a king boiling as a pot, and the banner of his army… came from the north." (Gill)
- **The second vision indicates the *contents* of Jeremiah's message**: judgment coming from the north. (Ellicott)

**v. 14: "Disaster from the north will be poured out on all who live in the land."**

- **"Out of the north an evil shall break forth"** — Babylon is meant (though geographically northeast, invading armies descended from the north because the Arabian Desert blocked a direct eastern approach). A minority view holds this refers to the Scythians. (Constable; Gill; Ellicott)
- **"Shall break forth"** (Hebrew "shall be opened" or "loosed") — what was previously bound and hindered by Providence is now released. (Gill; Constable)

**v. 15: "I am about to summon all the clans and kingdoms of the north… Their kings will come and set up their thrones at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem."**

- **"All the families of the kingdoms of the north"** = the various peoples under Nebuchadnezzar's jurisdiction. God "calls" them by "putting it into their hearts to come." (Gill)
- **"Setting a throne at the gates"** is a figure for establishing sovereignty and administering judgment. The city gates were "the ordinary places where justice was administered." The enemies would "assume the reigns of government" and lay the whole country under their own laws. (Clarke, quoted in Enduring Word; Constable)
- **This is a massive invasion**: not one enemy but many kingdoms, besieging Jerusalem and all the cities of Judah. (Constable)

**v. 16: "I will pronounce My judgments against them for all their wickedness, because they have forsaken Me to burn incense to other gods and to worship the works of their own hands."**

- **"Against them"** — against the people of Judah, not the invaders from the north. The Babylonians are God's instrument of judgment. (Gill)
- **The specific sins**: (1) forsaking the LORD (covenant unfaithfulness), (2) burning incense to other gods, (3) worshipping the works of their own hands (idolatry). These violated the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. (Constable; Gill)
- **The main reason** for coming judgment is chronic idolatry. (Enduring Word)

---

## Verses 17–19: God Commands Jeremiah to Be Steadfast

**v. 17: "Get yourself ready. Stand up and tell them everything that I command you. Do not be intimidated by them, or I will terrify you before them."**

- **"Gird up thy loins"** (literal Hebrew) — an allusion to the Eastern custom of gathering up long garments with a belt for quick action. It means "prepare for vigorous action." (Gill; Constable; cf. Exodus 12:11; Luke 12:35; 1 Peter 1:13)
- **"Lest I dismay [confound/terrify] you before them"** — a sobering warning. If Jeremiah gave way to fear of men, God Himself would become his adversary and give him real cause for terror. God cannot use a coward. The disobedient believer "not only fears people, but… also has God to fear because God becomes his… adversary." (Constable; Ellicott; Enduring Word)

**v. 18: "Now behold, this day I have made you like a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls against the whole land—against the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land."**

- **Three metaphors of impregnability**: a fortified (defenced) city, an iron pillar, and bronze (brasen) walls. All three convey invincibility, constancy, and immovability. "Jeremiah would not be popular in his day. His greatness was 'not his fame, but his faithfulness.'" (Gill; Constable / Wood)
- **Jeremiah certainly did not *feel* like any of these things** — he was a tender-hearted young man. But God's word was true, and he needed to believe it and act on it. (Enduring Word)
- **"Against the whole land"** — the opposition would come from every quarter: kings, princes (officials), priests, and common people. All classes would unite against him. (Gill; Constable)
- **Kidner**: "To this thin-skinned young man, his description in terms of battlements and heavy metal might have seemed a wild exaggeration, but in fact it proved an understatement. He would hold out against all comers for over forty years, outdoing any fortress under siege." (Quoted in Enduring Word)

**v. 19: "They will fight against you but will never overcome you, since I am with you to deliver you," declares the LORD.**

- **"They shall fight against thee… but they shall not prevail"** — this double promise proved literally true over Jeremiah's gruelling 40-year ministry. He was chained, flogged, thrown into a cistern, threatened with death, and his scroll was burned — but his enemies never overcame him. (Enduring Word; Constable)
- The Targum adds: "that they may hide the words of thy prophecy" — the enemies would fight to silence Jeremiah's message. (Gill)
- **"I am with you to deliver you"** — the same promise given in v. 8 is repeated, forming an inclusio around the call narrative. "For Jeremiah as for us, His way in general is not to stop the fight but to stand by the fighter." (Constable / Kidner)
- **Constable's application**: "Jeremiah's calling was not really that unusual. God has also chosen every Christian before the foundation of the world (Rom 8:29–30; Eph 1:4). He has chosen us to follow Him faithfully… He has also called every Christian to announce His Word (Matt 28:19)… And He has promised to be with us." (Constable)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Predestination and Election (v. 5)

- **Reformed (Calvinist) reading** — John Gill reads v. 5 as strong proof of unconditional election: God's "knowing" Jeremiah is "not merely by his omniscience… but with such a knowledge as had special love and affection joined with it… and predestinates them unto eternal life… before the foundation of the world, even from all eternity." (Gill)
- **John Piper** (Reformed Baptist) similarly emphasises God's sovereign choice: "Your life is rooted in the unshakable, sovereign purposes of God. You have been chosen and consecrated and formed and appointed for a great purpose." (Desiring God)
- **Arminian/Wesleyan reading** — though I could not retrieve a direct Wesleyan commentary on this passage, the traditional Arminian approach would read "I knew you" as God's foreknowledge of Jeremiah's free response, and "I set you apart" as a call conditioned on that foreknowledge. (Unable to confirm via seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu due to search limits.)
- **The Ellicott commentary** (Anglican) treats the predestination language straightforwardly as individual election to office without pressing it into a larger soteriological framework, noting that predestination was familiar in the OT and also in Assyrian royal ideology (King Assurbanipal claimed the gods "in the body of his mother have made him to rule Assyria"). (Ellicott)

### The "Foe from the North" (vv. 14–15)

- **Traditional majority view**: Babylon. This is held by Gill, Constable, Enduring Word (Guzik), and most traditional commentators. Babylon lay geographically northeast but invaded from the north due to desert barriers.
- **Minority scholarly view**: The Scythians. Constable notes that "a few" think this refers to the Scythians. This view is associated with some 19th–20th century critical scholarship. (Constable; Harrison)

### On the Nature of Prophetic Calling

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** — David Guzik (Enduring Word, though broadly evangelical) emphasises the visionary and experiential aspects: God "touched" Jeremiah's mouth in a real spiritual experience, and the visions were "training" for prophetic sight. Application is strongly personal: "When God calls us to serve, our feelings of inadequacy… don't change His call." (Enduring Word)
- **Baptist** — Spurgeon stresses the priority of *seeing* over *speaking*: the preacher must have an impression on his own soul before he can make an impression on others. The call must be personal and inwardly real. (Spurgeon)
- **Dispensational/Evangelical** — Constable stresses the historical-grammatical meaning, the fulfillment of covenant curses, and the parallel between Jeremiah's call and the Christian's call to witness. The application is to faithful proclamation more than to personal prophetic experience.

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

- I was unable to retrieve specific Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) commentaries on Jeremiah 1 due to search/fetch limits. Catholic commentaries (such as Haydock) traditionally read v. 5 as supporting the sanctity of life in the womb and the doctrine of God's foreknowledge, and v. 10 may be read in connection with Jeremiah's role prefiguring Christ's prophetic office. Orthodox readings often draw connections between Jeremiah's call and the liturgical theme of prophetic vocation.

### Lutheran Reading

- I was unable to retrieve specific Lutheran commentary (lcms.org, 1517.org) on this chapter due to search limits. Lutheran exegesis traditionally emphasises the *Word* character of Jeremiah's commission — "I have put My words in your mouth" — as the basis for the doctrine of the means of grace: God works through His spoken Word.

### Modern Scholarship

- **NET Bible notes** (netbible.org) would typically discuss the Hebrew wordplay in vv. 11–12, the dating issues around Josiah's 13th year, and text-critical issues in the LXX vs. MT. (Unable to fetch directly.)
- **Bible Odyssey** (bibleodyssey.org) would place Jeremiah's call in its ancient Near Eastern context, noting parallels with Assyrian royal election language. (Unable to fetch directly.)
